procedural_history.impugned_order: Orders of the Punjab High Court dated September 24, 1956, and September 26, 1956.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant filed a petition under Art. 226 of the Constitution in the Punjab High Court challenging the legality of his detention. He was permitted to argue that sub-s. (I) of s. 11 of the Preventive Detention Act was unconstitutional. A Division Bench of the Punjab High Court held that sub-s. (1) of s. 11 of the Act was constitutional on September 24, 1956. A single Judge of the High Court then dismissed the appellant's petition on merits on September 26, 1956. The appellant unsuccessfully sought leave to appeal to the Supreme Court from the Punjab High Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant moved the Supreme Court and obtained special leave to appeal from the Punjab High Court's orders of September 24 and 26, 1956. Before that, the appellant had also filed a petition in the Supreme Court challenging the legality of his detention and seeking a writ of habeas corpus, but this petition was dismissed.

issue.issue_text: Whether sub-section (1) of section 11 of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 is unconstitutional as it offends against Article 22(4)(a) of the Constitution.

facts: The appellant was detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950.
His case was referred to an Advisory Board, which reported that there was sufficient cause for his detention.
Following the Board's report, the Central Government, acting under Section 11(1) of the Act, confirmed the detention and ordered it to continue for twelve months.
law: Article 22(4)(a) of the Constitution states that no law shall authorize detention for more than three months unless an Advisory Board reports before the end of the three months that there is, in its opinion, sufficient cause for 'such detention'.

Section 11(1) of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, allows the government to confirm a detention order and continue the detention for a period it deems fit, after the Advisory Board has reported that there is sufficient cause for the detention.
application: The core of the issue was the interpretation of the phrase 'such detention' in Article 22(4)(a).

The appellant argued that 'such detention' referred to detention for a period *longer than three months*. Therefore, the Advisory Board must specifically report that there is sufficient cause for detention *for more than three months*. Since Section 11(1) did not require this specific finding, it was unconstitutional.
The government (respondent) argued that 'such detention' referred to the *preventive detention itself*, as mentioned at the beginning of Article 22(4).
The Supreme Court agreed with the government's interpretation.
The Court reasoned that the role of the Advisory Board is only to determine if there is sufficient cause for the detention itself, not to decide on the duration of the detention.

The Constitution sets a three-month limit on detention without the Board's approval. Once the Board reports that there is sufficient cause for the detention, the constitutional requirement is met, and the government is then empowered by Section 11(1) of the Act to confirm the order and fix the period of detention (up to the maximum allowed by the Act).
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's challenge, holding that Section 11(1) of the Preventive Detention Act is not unconstitutional. The Court concluded that the phrase 'such detention' in Article 22(4)(a) refers to the preventive detention itself, not the period of detention. Therefore, the Advisory Board's duty is to opine on the sufficiency of the cause for detention, not its duration, which is a decision for the government to make after receiving the Board's report.

issue.issue_text: Whether the non-disclosure of facts and particulars by the government on grounds of public interest under Article 22(6) of the Constitution prevents the detainee from making an effective representation.

facts: The government detained the appellant and provided grounds for the detention.
The government refused to disclose certain facts and particulars, such as dates, persons, and places, related to the grounds for detention.
The government justified this non-disclosure by stating that revealing these details would be against the public interest, as permitted under Article 22(6) of the Constitution.
The appellant argued that this non-disclosure deprived him of his right to make an effective representation against his detention, a right guaranteed by Article 22(5).
law: Article 22(5) of the Constitution confers two rights on a detainee: 1) the right to be informed of the grounds for detention, and 2) the right to be afforded the earliest opportunity to make a representation against the order.

Article 22(6) of the Constitution provides an exception to this, stating that the detaining authority is not required to disclose facts which it considers to be against the public interest to disclose.
The Supreme Court held that the right to make a representation under Article 22(5) is subject to the limitation mentioned in Article 22(6).
The right of the detaining authority to withhold information under Article 22(6) is a privilege that limits the detainee's right to be furnished with all facts and particulars.
application: The Court determined that the government had exercised its privilege under Article 22(6) to withhold certain details on the grounds of public interest.

Because the right to representation is subject to this privilege, the appellant cannot argue that the absence of these specific facts and particulars prevented him from making an effective representation.
The Court noted that this conclusion stands, provided there is no question of "mala fides" (bad faith) on the part of the detaining authority.

In this specific case, the Court also found that the grounds that were provided, even without the withheld details, were sufficient to give the appellant an opportunity to exercise his right to make a representation.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the appellant's argument, concluding that when the government validly invokes its privilege under Article 22(6) to not disclose facts on grounds of public interest, the detainee cannot claim that this non-disclosure prevented them from making an effective representation under Article 22(5).

arguments.issue_text: Whether sub-section (1) of section 11 of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 is unconstitutional as it offends against Article 22(4)(a) of the Constitution.
appellant_arguments: The phrase 'such detention' in Article 22(4)(a) of the Constitution refers specifically to 'detention for a longer period than three months'.
Therefore, the Advisory Board must report that there is sufficient cause for detention for a period longer than three months, not merely for the detention itself.
As the Act's provisions authorize detention for more than three months without this specific finding from the Board, they are unconstitutional (ultra vires).
respondent_arguments: The phrase 'such detention' is capable of two meanings: detention simpliciter (preventive detention itself) or detention for a period longer than three months.
The correct interpretation is detention simpliciter.

The phrase 'such detention' in Article 22(4) is intended to refer to preventive detention in general, distinguishing it from other types of detention mentioned in Articles 22(1) and 22(2), without reference to its duration.

cases.case_name: A. K. Gopalan v. The State of Madras
cases.principle: To interpret Article 22(4) as meaning that a law providing for preventive detention for more than three months must establish an advisory board that reports on the sufficiency of the cause for detention before three months expire. It was also cited for the principle that the advisory board is the constitutional machinery for reviewing preventive detention orders.

cases.case_name: Lawrence Joachim Joseph D'Souza v. The State of Bombay
cases.principle: That under the Constitution, detention cannot exceed three months unless an Advisory Board finds sufficient cause for it, and that detention for a longer period can only be made based on the Board's report.

cases.case_name: State of Bombay v. Atma Ram Sridhar Vaidya
cases.principle: That under the Constitution, detention cannot exceed three months unless an Advisory Board finds sufficient cause for it, and that detention for a longer period can only be made based on the Board's report.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A law authorizing preventive detention for more than three months is constitutionally valid under Article 22(4)(a) if it mandates that the government can only fix the period of detention after receiving a report from an Advisory Board.
obiter: If the intention of the Constitution was that a law made on the subject of preventive detention had to be tested on the touchstone of reasonableness, then it would not have troubled itself by expressly making provision in article 22 about the precise scope of the limitation subject to which such a law could be made.

The provision being in the nature of a protection or safeguard, I must naturally lean towards the interpretation which is favourable to the subject and which is also in accord with the object in view.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court held that the government's constitutional privilege to withhold information in the public interest under Article 22(6) is a direct limitation on the detainee's right to receive particulars for making a representation under Article 22(5). Therefore, a detainee cannot claim their right to make an effective representation has been violated by non-disclosure, unless it can be proven that the government acted in bad faith (mala fides).
legal_tests_applied: The court applied a balancing test where the detainee's right to information for representation under Article 22(5) is read as being explicitly "subject to" the government's privilege of non-disclosure in the public interest under Article 22(6).

The court applied a test for mala fides, stating that the detainee can only challenge the non-disclosure of particulars if it can be shown that the executive was "actuated by any ulterior purposes other than those mentioned in the order of detention."
why_appellant_lost: The court rejected the argument that 'such detention' in Article 22(4)(a) refers specifically to detention longer than three months. It adopted the reasoning that since the Constitution requires the Advisory Board's report to be made *before* the expiry of three months, its purpose must be to opine on the detention itself, not on a future period beyond three months.

The appellant's argument that non-disclosure of particulars prevented an effective representation failed because the right to receive such particulars is not absolute. The court found that this right is explicitly limited by the privilege granted to the state under Article 22(6).

The court held that once the government validly exercises its privilege of non-disclosure under Article 22(6), "the appellant cannot be heard to say, apart from the question of mala fides, that the grounds did not disclose the necessary facts or particulars, or that in the absence of such facts or particulars, he was not in a position to make an effective representation."

The appellant failed to prove that the government's decision to withhold information was made in bad faith, with the court stating, "On the materials placed before us, we unhesitatingly hold that no mala fides have been established."

On the facts of the case, the court concluded that the grounds provided were adequate, stating, "We are of the opinion that in the present case the grounds furnished to the appellant, though not as precise and definite as might be desired, gave him a sufficient opportunity of exercising his right under cl. (5) of Art. 22 of the Constitution."
why_respondent_won: The respondent's interpretation of 'such detention' in Article 22(4)(a) as referring to preventive detention in general (simpliciter) was accepted. This view was supported by the structural logic of the Constitution, which requires the Advisory Board to report within the initial three-month period.
The government's right to withhold information under Article 22(6) was affirmed as a constitutional privilege that qualifies the detainee's right to be furnished with particulars.

The court relied on precedent, specifically *Lawrence Joachim Joseph D' Souza v. The State of Bombay*, which established that "the right of the detenu to be furnished with facts or particulars was subject to the limitation mentioned in cl. (6)."

The court affirmed the principle from *The State of Bombay v. Atma Ram Sridhar Vaidya* that the satisfaction of the detaining authority is paramount and cannot be challenged, except on grounds of mala fides, as long as the grounds have a rational connection to the objects of the Act.
policy_considerations: The court acknowledged the principle of interpreting constitutional safeguards in a manner favorable to the individual, quoting with approval the view that "The provision being in the nature of a protection or safeguard, I must naturally lean towards the interpretation which is favourable to the subject and which is also in accord with the object in view."

The reasoning reflects a balance between the individual's right to liberty and the state's interest in national security and public order, ultimately holding that the constitutional text explicitly allows for the curtailment of the right to information when public interest is at stake.
